name: Audience-Reactive Installations
title: Audience-Reactive Installations
answer: Audience-reactive installations are artworks in which sensors and AI systems change sound, light, projection, or physical movement in response to the people present. They sit within interactive and experiential art, where the audience is not a passive viewer but a co-producer of the piece. The scope includes gallery environments, public spaces, stage performances, and site-specific works that use real-time input such as motion, gaze, voice, or physiological signals. These installations often blend generative imagery, spatial audio, and robotics, and they are documented as live systems rather than fixed objects.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Most audience-reactive installations run on a local machine or small cluster in the venue, because low latency matters more than cloud scale. A typical setup includes cameras, depth sensors, microphones, or lidar feeding a computer with a strong GPU, which then drives projectors, LED panels, speakers, or motors. Some works use edge devices like Jetson modules or dedicated media servers, while cloud services are reserved for non-real-time tasks such as training or content pre-generation. Reliable power, cooling, and network isolation are common practical concerns.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is usually done by combining computer vision, audio analysis, and generative models in a tight loop. A pose estimation or face tracking model extracts features from the audience, and those features are mapped to parameters of a generative image, video, or sound model. The mapping is often designed by the artist rather than learned, so the system behaves in legible, repeatable ways. Some installations use reinforcement learning or evolutionary algorithms to let the piece adapt over the course of an exhibition, but the core loop is sensing, interpreting, and rendering within a fraction of a second.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on the people being sensed. Installations that capture faces, voices, or biometric data may trigger privacy and data protection duties, especially in public or semi-public spaces, and clear signage or opt-out routes are common practice. The generated output can raise copyright questions if models were trained on unlicensed work, and provenance records should note which models and datasets were used. Liability for harm, such as strobe effects, loud sound, or physical movement, sits with the operator, so risk assessments and insurance are part of production.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward more personal and persistent responses, where an installation remembers a returning visitor or coordinates many people at once without central control. On-device inference is making it easier to run complex models without sending data off site, which reduces latency and privacy exposure. Artists are also exploring shared agency, where the audience can see and adjust the rules of the system, and curators are beginning to treat these works as living systems that need maintenance, versioning, and documentation over time.
